extracted.intended_audience: students and professors of a Catholic university (evening classes), especially medical students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, delivering, and evaluating university evening lectures and instruction, emphasizing active learning, steady attendance, disciplined exercises, substantive content over display, and the proper professional limits of medical practice in relation to religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary object of lectures — to teach (not exhibit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary object of lectures is to teach; lectures should 'impart something definite' to those who attend rather than serve as exhibitions or mere displays of eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ordinary teaching and occasional celebratory oratorical displays (e.g., inaugural or terminal lectures). Exhibitions aim to attract or astonish and are 'intended for seeing rather than for hearing' and should be rare; the normal mode of a lecture is a business-like mutual undertaking between lecturer and listener ('I will speak, if you will listen').

rubrics_metrics.name: Active engagement and mastery (not passive reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge must not be passively received but 'actually and actively entered into, embraced, mastered' — the mind must go halfway to meet incoming material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer catechetical instruction: questioning, requiring repetition, examination — the lecturer should not let students go until there is proof that they know, not merely that they heard. Anti-pattern: indolent or passive hearing that produces no positive or permanent mental effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steady, persevering attendance over mere numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Attendance is 'satisfactory' when it is steady and persevering rather than simply numerous or noisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audiences by the character and purpose of attendees (those who come 'on business' to gain information from authorities) rather than raw headcount or spectacle; a small, diligent audience may be better evidence of success than a large, casual one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on novelty and spectacle; prefer patience and routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on sudden, startling effects or a 'stimulating system' to attract attention; build influence by 'slow, silent, penetrating' steady work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained weekly lectures, perseverance in face of low initial attendance, and gradual word-of-mouth growth create enduring followings; sudden popularity ('a blaze among the stubble') often dies away quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desultory reading and popular lectures insufficient for deep education
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics' institutes, popular literature, and desultory reading can provide amusement and information but generally fail to secure 'permanent advantage' or the formation of intellectual habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sources are valuable as supplements but not substitutes for disciplined teaching; anti-patterns include accumulation of loose ideas without principles, leading to shallow or fleeting 'knowledge' (the warning that 'a little learning is a dangerous thing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical, laborious teaching to form habits of order and system
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should produce a 'formation of mind' — a habit of order and system that refers new knowledge to what is already known and sets up principles as centres of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether courses encourage systematic thought, integration of facts into principles, and long-term intellectual structure rather than isolated facts or rhetorical flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete intellectual exercises to build discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective teaching uses specific exercises (translation, memorization, mastering definitions, proving propositions, analyzing speeches, writing critiques) to cultivate accuracy, memory, discrimination, acuteness, caution, and logical precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess curricula by presence of tasks such as: construing and translating languages, getting up a chapter of history, proving Euclidean propositions, mastering major arguments, analyzing speeches, and composing critiques — these are practical means to develop critical faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over eloquence — do not substitute style for matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquent diction or rhetorical display should not substitute for matter or proof; eloquence that is merely show fails as teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware terminal or ornamental lectures that prioritize display. Prefer instruction that provides evidence and logical proof; treat eloquence as secondary and not a measure of true learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture as a mutual contract: responsibilities of lecturer and learner
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures are a cooperative enterprise: the lecturer undertakes to teach and the listeners undertake to come to learn — each has duties to fulfill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational arrangements should remind attendees of this mutual commitment (mementos in arrangements); evaluate success by whether both parties act on their respective responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly distinguish pedagogical aims from occasional public exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between lectures intended for steady instruction and those intended to influence public opinion or to display academic prestige; both have valid but distinct aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept occasional extraordinary lectures for public influence, but do not make such exhibitions the norm of academic proceedings; measure extraordinary lectures by their success at attracting attention, ordinary lectures by their success at imparting definite knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should attend with purpose ('on business') not mere curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners ought to come to classes with the intention to gain knowledge, not merely out of curiosity or to 'see how things were going on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess student engagement and motivation; arrangements and teaching styles should cultivate a sense that attendance is a task of learning rather than casual entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional boundary: medicine must yield to higher moral/religious duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical science concerns bodily health but is not the highest science; in cases of conflict, bodily health may have to give way to moral or religious obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Sister of Charity who remains with the sick despite medical risk may be right to subordinate health to religious duty. Evaluate medical advice within the broader context of moral and religious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid professional overreach and the usurpation of other domains
rubrics_metrics.description: All professions have a tendency toward exclusiveness and to intrude into other spheres (politics, religion, etc.); such usurpations, even if in good faith, must be checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that lawyers, bureaucrats, literati, or scientists may attempt to make religion a province of their expertise; maintain appropriate limits and deference to higher-order disciplines where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the fallacy 'what is true is lawful' across sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth asserted within one science does not automatically authorize corresponding action in another domain; 'what is true in one science is not dictated to us according to another science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize domain-specific authority: a medical fact does not automatically settle questions of duty or policy in moral/religious contexts. Evaluate claims with attention to disciplinary limits and hierarchy of ends.
